literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The past two days have been dominated by a wonderfully unlikely Booker winner, and around him there are some good pieces on narrators, sentences and the craft of writing.

Let's begin with M John Harrison, who at eighty-one is the oldest writer ever to win the Booker Prize. Three interviews have appeared, and together they give a lovely picture of a man who is delighted, a little baffled, and entirely himself. In The Bookseller, he talks about age and about his long refusal of genre labels, and he says, rather beautifully, "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." The i Paper goes for a more mischievous note, with his line that he is going to die soon and so can do what he likes. It is the sort of remark that makes late recognition sound less like a coronation and more like a licence. The Irish Times is warmer and more intimate, describing how he lies awake most of the night thinking, "This is extraordinary." Any of these would work well to read aloud to a class, because they show a writer speaking plainly about what success feels like when it arrives very late.

As for the book itself, The Indian Express calls it a post-apocalyptic satire, and presents the win as the moment the New Weird goes mainstream. The same paper has a useful explainer on that term, which Harrison is closely associated with. If your students have never met the New Weird, it places his unsettling, unusual fiction within a literary tradition, and is a good starting point. The Guardian, in an editorial, sees the win as a new frontier for science fiction, setting the novel within the wider history of the genre. And Open Magazine has a piece on what it calls the subversive humanity of the winning novel, although only the headline was available to me, so I can say only that it points to a book with a human heart beneath its strangeness.

Moving from prizes to voices, The Guardian reviews the audiobook of Ben Lerner's Transcription, narrated by Seth Numrich. It follows an anxious, unnamed narrator who travels to interview his former mentor, a ninety-year-old German writer. The reviewer describes a layered tale of memory, family and storytelling, a meditation on memory for the smartphone era. It is a reminder that an unnamed, nervous narrator can be as gripping as any thriller detective, and that a good reader's voice can shape how we hear him.

For those who love prose as music, The Paris Review's Daily has its November bookmarks, a selection of passages underlined in new releases, under the title "A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room." It is a pleasure to dip into, because it puts the sentence itself at the centre. And if you are looking ahead to winter reading, The Guardian has a round-up of new paperbacks for November and December, including books by Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike. It also mentions an experimental novel about a German actor, and a study of how the arts can boost health, which I suspect you might enjoy for your own reasons as much as for your students'.

On the craft of writing, Literary Hub offers two thoughtful pieces. In the first, a poet describes turning her second collection, Future Tense, into a page-turner. The book is a memoir in verse that documents three years of struggle, and her question is how poetry can create narrative pull without losing what makes it poetry. It might be a useful companion to any lesson on verse that tells a story. The second is a gentle, rather encouraging essay, first printed in Lit Hub's Craft of Writing newsletter, arguing that everybody's first drafts are bad, and are meant to be. It compares an early novel to a lumpy handmade scarf, which is an image your students may find reassuring when they face a blank page.

Literary Hub also has two personal essays that stay with the voice rather than the argument. One is about the absence of words to comfort the writer during her pregnancy, and why it matters to archive Black motherhood. It is about how stories hold and console us, and what is lost when there are none to turn to. The other, simply titled "Dogs", opens with a young woman's solo train journey to Prague, hungover and weighed down. The text I had was very short, so I cannot say where it goes, but the narrative voice is vivid from the first lines, and it may be worth reading for that alone.

Finally, something to look forward to. Equator magazine is running a reading group in twenty twenty-seven on Roberto Bolaño's 2666, following a summer edition on Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts. If you have been putting that great, demanding novel off for years, this is an invitation to finally tackle it in company, which may make it easier.

That is all for today, Yamuna. I hope your morning is gentle, and that your next book finds you at exactly the right moment, whatever your age.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The Booker Prize is still dominating the literary conversation this Saturday, and around it there are some lovely pieces on narrators, sentences and the stubborn business of getting words onto a page.

Let us begin with M John Harrison, who at eighty-one is the oldest writer ever to win the Booker. Four different outlets have been talking to him or about him, and what struck me is how much of it is about voice, his own as much as his fiction's.

The Bookseller has an interview on age and on his refusal of genre labels. His line is, "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." It is a small, disarming remark, and I think it would work well with older students, who tend to imagine that writers arrive fully formed and elderly. Here is a man who has been writing for decades and still feels, inwardly, like a young person at the start.

The i Paper catches him in a more mischievous mood. Its headline has him saying, "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." There is something bracing about that, a kind of freedom granted by late recognition, and it fits a writer who has spent his career declining to be filed neatly on any shelf. The Irish Times gives us the warmer, more private side. He describes lying awake for much of the night, thinking, "This is extraordinary." Put the three together and you get a lovely triptych: the playful one, the defiant one, and the one who cannot quite believe his luck.

Now to the book itself, and what the prize means. The Indian Express calls it a post-apocalyptic satire and presents the win as the New Weird reaching the mainstream. That is the most substantial account of this year's prize that I have seen. The same paper has a companion explainer on the New Weird, the term Harrison is associated with, and it is useful if you want to place his unusual, unsettling fiction within a literary tradition rather than simply calling it strange. If your première students enjoy dystopias, this could be a way in. The New Weird is a kind of writing that borrows the furniture of fantasy and science fiction, but is more interested in unease and atmosphere than in rules and maps. Treat that as a loose description rather than a definition, as I am working only from the explainer's framing.

The Guardian's editorial takes a wider view. It calls the win "a new frontier for science fiction" and places the novel within the longer history and development of the genre. I find that framing interesting, because it suggests that the old wall between literary fiction and genre fiction may be getting a little lower. Harrison, of course, rejects genre labels altogether, so the editorial and the author are, in a gentle way, approaching the same question from opposite sides. One says the genre has moved forward. The other says he never wanted to live in it. There is a nice classroom discussion hidden there about who gets to decide what a book is.

There is also a piece in Open Magazine, headed "Catastrophic Effect: The subversive humanity of the new Booker winner." I should be honest that only the headline reached me, so I cannot tell you much about the argument. But the phrase "subversive humanity" is a suggestive one. It hints that beneath the apocalyptic satire there is warmth, even tenderness, which would match the personality that comes through in those interviews.

Let me turn from prizes to narrators, which I know is close to your heart. The Guardian has reviewed the audiobook of Ben Lerner's Transcription, narrated by Seth Numrich, and describes it as a meditation on memory for the smartphone era. The story follows an unnamed, anxious narrator who travels to interview his former mentor, a ninety-year-old German writer. From the review, it is a layered tale about memory, family and storytelling. I like the setup very much: a nervous younger man, an elderly writer, and a conversation that has to be captured, remembered and retold. A book that is, in a sense, about the unreliability of every kind of recording. Hearing it read aloud, rather than on the page, adds another layer to that theme, since the voice in your ear belongs to an actor performing someone who is anxious about how to listen. If you are a lover of audiobooks, or if you want to introduce your students to the idea of a narrator who barely knows himself, this seems well worth a listen.

On the subject of sentences, The Paris Review's Daily has its November Bookmarks, titled "A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room." It is a selection of passages underlined in new releases. I love this format, because it gives you the book through its language rather than through plot summaries. You read a handful of lines and you know at once whether a writer's music is for you. It might even be a good source for a warm-up exercise: put a single striking sentence on the board, and ask students what the writer is doing with rhythm, with word choice, with the position of the verb. Passages chosen by other readers because they could not resist underlining them have a certain authority.

Literary Hub has a personal essay called "Dogs" which opens with a young woman's solo train journey to Prague, hungover and weighed down. The text I have is very short, so I cannot say where the essay goes. But that opening image is vivid, a young person, a train, a heavy head and a heavier heart, and it suggests a narrator with a clear, slightly rueful voice. Sometimes a first paragraph is all one needs to decide to keep reading.

That leads naturally to the craft of writing, where Literary Hub is generous today. One piece asks, "Can You Write a Poetry Collection That's a Page-Turner?" A poet describes making her second collection, Future Tense, a memoir in verse that documents three years of struggle, into something with real narrative pull. I find the question fascinating, because we tend to think of poems as things to be savoured slowly, one at a time. But a sequence of poems can also carry us forward like a novel, wanting to know what happens next. If you ever teach poetry alongside fiction, it could be a good way to show students that the boundary between the two is more porous than the syllabus might suggest.

Another Literary Hub piece, first printed in its Craft of Writing newsletter, is called "Everybody's First Drafts Are Bad." The argument is that first drafts are supposed to be rough, and it compares an early novel to a lumpy handmade scarf. I do love that image. It is affectionate rather than harsh, and it treats the roughness as evidence of something real having been made by hand. For students who freeze in front of a blank page because they fear writing badly, this is the kind of reassurance that can be read aloud in class, and perhaps be followed by a ten-minute writing exercise in which nobody is allowed to edit.

Also on Literary Hub, there is a personal essay titled "What We Lose When We Don't Archive Black Motherhood." The writer describes the absence of words to comfort her during pregnancy, and makes the case for why archiving Black motherhood matters. It is a thoughtful piece about how stories hold and console us, and about what happens when the stories we need have not been written down or passed on. It reminds us that literature is not only a source of pleasure or of analysis, but sometimes a form of company in a difficult hour. I would say it connects with your interest in novels that teach us about lives we have not lived, though here the lesson comes in the form of a personal essay, rather than fiction.

Finally, some reading to look forward to. The Guardian has its round-up of the best new paperbacks for November and December, with Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike among the names. It also picks out an experimental novel about a German actor, and a study of how the arts can boost health. That last one seems timely for anyone who has ever felt that a concert or an exhibition did them more good than a day off. With the dark evenings drawing in above the Grésivaudan, paperbacks are, I think, the right shape of book for the season: light enough to carry, and cheap enough to take a chance on.

And for readers who like a long-term project, Literary Hub reports that Equator magazine is running a reading group in twenty twenty-seven on Roberto Bolaño's 2666. This follows a summer edition on Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts. The idea is simply to give people the company they need to finally tackle a demanding novel, and I think there is something very appealing in that. Some books are best read as a shared expedition, with other people to say, "Are you still with me?" along the way. If 2666 has been sitting unread on a shelf, the new year might be the moment.

So, a morning of late triumphs, anxious narrators, rough first drafts and big books waiting patiently on shelves. I hope you find a good sentence to carry with you today, Yamuna.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. This morning's art news has a pleasingly literary bent, with a good deal of it about how paintings, music and stories lean on one another, and a few things close to home.

Let me start in Grenoble. L'essentiel reports that the Musée de Grenoble has a new exhibition, though all we have is the headline, so I can't yet tell you the artists, the dates or the theme. It's worth a look at the museum's own page before you plan a visit. Actu.fr also reports that a work from the Fête des Lumières in Lyon is travelling to Isère, and its piece sets out where and when you can see it. The text is brief, but it's a public artwork on your doorstep. And since it's Saturday, mesinfos has its guide to what's on in Grenoble this weekend, from Friday the thirteenth to Sunday the fifteenth of November. Again it's only a headline, but it may turn up an exhibition or a concert worth the drive down from Les Adrets.

Now to the stories where art and writing meet, which I suspect you'll enjoy most. On BBC Radio 4's Front Row, there's a review of Jonathan Coe's novel Lessons in Harmony, which imagines the friendship between Ravel and Vaughan Williams. The same programme looks at Inside Bloomsbury, the Tate Britain exhibition on Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. So you get fiction, music and painting in one conversation. A second Front Row episode, forty-two minutes long, has China Miéville talking about writing The Rouse, a novel of one thousand, two hundred and sixty-four pages. It's an hour of listening for anyone who loves a writer explaining why a book needed to be that long. The same episode also covers Honey, a darkly comedic Cold War thriller from the makers of Killing Eve, which may suit your taste for thrillers.

Hyperallergic has two pieces in this vein. The first is about James Cahill's new book, which takes David Hockney's portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman as its starting point. It tells the story of two friends who shaped the cultural life of Los Angeles in the nineteen-sixties, so it's a painting opening onto a richly told human story. The second concerns El Museo del Barrio in New York, which is restaging Papo Colo's Octopus and Others, a show pairing text and image that was first seen four decades ago. It's a rare chance to see how a poet and an artist worked together, on the page and on the wall.

And in Paris, Beaux Arts Magazine highlights an exhibition called Nicolas Flamel, alchimiste de papier. It follows the legend of the alchemist from the philosopher's stone through to its echoes in the Harry Potter books. It's a lovely example of a real historical figure being gradually turned into fiction, which might even make a good classroom starting point.

Two stories this week concern famous paintings and what lies beneath their surface. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found an unprecedented technique, and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The report is only a short teaser, so we'll have to wait for the details, but it's a striking prospect. Hyperallergic, meanwhile, reports that scientists have found Rembrandt's Night Watch to be teeming with microbes, and they hope this invisible life will help explain some of the painting's mysteries. It's an odd and rather wonderful way of looking again at one of the most familiar canvases in the world.

Then there are artists being seen on their own terms. In Metz, Beaux Arts Magazine reports the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was a self-taught painter who worked as a cleaner, and the show aims to reveal the great painter behind the legend. It's a story of an overlooked artist finally being taken seriously, and I imagine it would make you want to read around her life too. Also in Paris, there's an exhibition on shunga, the Japanese erotic prints and paintings that were long kept out of sight for reasons of modesty. Beaux Arts Magazine describes their tentacular audacity, and it promises a fresh look at a body of work that deserves its place in art history.

From the Guardian's art and design pages come a few more. An immersive show at the National Library of Wales brings the landscapes of Sir Kyffin Williams to life, with his thick, palette-knifed paintings animated and set to music. If you like the Welsh hills, it sounds like an unusual way to meet them. In the Guardian's week in art, Turner Contemporary in Margate has a free display by Nicole Eisenman, which runs from today, the fourteenth of November, until the eleventh of April, and is described as witty and imaginative. The same roundup touches on Scottish Roman history and on work by Wolfgang Tillmans and Tracey Emin.

And finally, a lovely piece of oral history in the Guardian, a photo essay in which Teddy Trevor, now ninety, remembers the Australian sideshow tradition of his family and fellow showmen. Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now, as the title has it. The voices are vivid, and the characters feel as if they've stepped out of a novel.

That's the art news for today, Yamuna. I hope your weekend has a little colour in it.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the fourteenth of November, and today's art briefing begins close to home, then wanders through secrets hidden in famous paintings, and ends with a good many stories where art and writing run side by side.

Let me start in Grenoble, with a small warning: the local news is thinner than I would like. L'Essentiel media announces a new exhibition at the Musée de Grenoble, but all we have is the headline. I can't tell you the artists, the dates or the theme. Still, since it is your local museum, it is worth looking at the museum's own programme before the weekend is out, in case something there is worth a trip down into the city. In the same spirit, mesinfos has published its weekend guide for Grenoble, covering Friday the thirteenth to Sunday the fifteenth of November. Again, only the headline reached me, so I can't promise exhibitions or concerts, but as today is Saturday, it might be a useful thing to glance at over coffee.

Then there is a story from Actu.fr about a work from the Fête des Lumières in Lyon that is travelling to Isère. The article says where and when you can see it, though the details didn't come through to me. What I like about it is the idea of a piece made for the great Lyon festival of light finding a second life in our own department. If it turns out to be somewhere reachable from Les Adrets, it could make a pleasant evening out as the nights draw in.

Now to the paintings themselves, and to the idea that even the most famous canvases still have things to tell us. The most striking story this week comes from Beaux Arts Magazine, which reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly discovered an unprecedented technique, and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The piece I saw was only a short teaser, so I can't tell you what the technique is, or where the self-portrait is hiding. But it is a lovely thought. A fresco that millions of people have gazed at still keeps a private signature of its maker, tucked away until a restorer's careful hand finds it. For a teacher of literature there is something very familiar in that: the narrator who slips into the margins of his own story.

Staying with famous paintings, Hyperallergic has a piece titled "Rembrandt's Night Watch Is Alive!" Scientists have found that the painting is home to teeming microbes, and they hope this invisible life will help explain some of the painting's mysteries. I find that rather wonderful, and a little eerie. We think of the Night Watch as a great, solid, dark and golden picture of gathered figures, and yet on its surface there is a whole other crowd, far too small to see, living alongside the militia company. The article doesn't tell us here which mysteries the researchers hope to solve, but it is a fresh way of looking at a canvas we think we know.

From the secrets of old masters to a painter who was kept from sight by her own legend. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that in Metz, the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis opens, a painter who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was self-taught and had worked as a cleaner, and the exhibition's promise, in the magazine's words, is to reveal the great painter behind the legend. That phrase is the heart of it. Séraphine has long been a figure of story, the humble woman who painted in secret, and stories like that can quietly swallow the work. A full international retrospective is the chance to look at the paintings on their own terms, rather than through the charming myth. I think this would make a fine thing to put in front of your première students, who often like to ask who gets to be called an artist, and who decides.

The Guardian, meanwhile, brings us a very different way of meeting a painter. At the National Library of Wales there is an immersive show that animates the landscapes of Sir Kyffin Williams and sets them to music. Williams painted Wales in thick, rugged strokes of the palette knife, and now those surfaces move and breathe. It's interesting to wonder what happens to a painting when you give it time. A palette-knife landscape is all about the frozen moment, the weight of paint, and here it is turned into something you sit inside, with music beneath it. I can't say from the report how well it works, but the idea of walking into a Welsh hillside made of paint is an appealing one, and it feels almost like a poem set to a score.

That brings me, rather naturally, to the part of the briefing I suspect you will enjoy most, where painting, music and writing meet. The BBC Radio 4 programme Front Row has a review of Jonathan Coe's new novel, Lessons in Harmony, which is about the friendship between Ravel and Vaughan Williams. In the same episode, they cover the Inside Bloomsbury exhibition at Tate Britain, which looks at Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. So within a single programme you have a novel about two composers, and a gallery show about two painters, all of them bound up in friendship and in the way creative people sustain one another. I like the pairing a great deal. Coe is a novelist who writes warmly about friendship and about the English character, and here he is imagining the closeness of two musicians. Meanwhile Tate Britain is showing the domestic, shared world of two painters. It might be a good listen on a walk up in Belledonne.

The same Front Row team also has another episode, forty-two minutes long, that looks at Honey, a new darkly comedic Cold War thriller from the makers of Killing Eve. But the part I would point you towards is a conversation with China Miéville about writing The Rouse, a novel of one thousand, two hundred and sixty-four pages. That is a great deal of book. It will be interesting to hear a writer talk about what it takes to sustain a voice and a world across that length, and what it feels like to live with a story for so many pages. Whether you decide to read it, or simply enjoy hearing him talk about it, it feels like a conversation about the craft of narration, which is your territory.

Another piece that braids a painting with a human story comes from Hyperallergic. James Cahill has written a book that begins with David Hockney's portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. From that starting point, he tells the story of two friends who shaped the cultural life of Los Angeles in the nineteen-sixties. What I like in the description is that the painting is a doorway and not the destination. The portrait opens onto friendship, a city and an era, and that is just what a good novel does with a single character. It sounds like a book that could make a decade of Californian culture feel as intimate as a dinner party.

Also in Hyperallergic, there is a story about the meeting of poetry and image. El Museo del Barrio is restaging Papo Colo's show Octopus and Others, which pairs text and image, and was first shown four decades ago. The piece calls it an artist-poet collaboration with alchemical possibilities, and I like the phrase. We are told it is a rare chance to see how a poet and an artist worked together on the page and on the wall. The report doesn't say who the poet was, and I wouldn't want to guess, but the question underneath it is a lovely one for a classroom: what happens when words and pictures are not illustrating each other, but really thinking together?

Speaking of alchemy, here is a story that crosses from history into fiction in a most direct way. Beaux Arts Magazine writes about an exhibition called Nicolas Flamel, alchimiste de papier. It traces the legend of the alchemist, from the philosopher's stone to its echoes in the Harry Potter saga. The magazine's own headline adds a wry twist, suggesting that behind the legend of the alchemist lay the fabulous destiny of a property investor. I couldn't tell you more about the exhibition, such as where it is or how long it runs, but the idea is delicious: a real figure, a piece of paper history, a myth that grew and grew, and then a modern children's novel that borrowed his name. It's a neat example of how a story travels across the centuries, and perhaps a way to show students that fiction has always been in conversation with the past.

Now a few stories from further afield, each worth a moment. In Paris, Beaux Arts Magazine describes an exhibition on shunga, the Japanese erotic prints and paintings that were long kept out of sight, out of modesty. The headline speaks of the tentacular audacity of the genre. What interests me is the phrase about being hidden. It's a reminder that the history of art is also a history of what was put away in a drawer, and that looking again, with fresh eyes and good context, can change how we understand a whole culture.

The Guardian, in its art and design pages, has a photo essay with a title straight from a fairground barker: "Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!" It follows Teddy Trevor, who is now ninety, as he remembers the Australian sideshow tradition of his family and fellow showmen, calling him the last of the great Australian showmen. It's a piece of oral history, full of voices and vivid characters. I suspect it might be the sort of thing you read aloud to yourself, just to enjoy the patter.

And lastly, the Guardian's week in art offers a handful of things to look out for. From today, the fourteenth of November, until the eleventh of April, Turner Contemporary in Margate hosts a free display by Nicole Eisenman, which the paper describes as witty and imaginative. The same roundup touches on Scottish Roman history, and on work by Wolfgang Tillmans and Tracey Emin. It's a useful little map of the British art scene, if you are planning a trip across the Channel in the months ahead.

So that is the week: secrets inside the old masters, a painter finally seen for herself, and a good many friendships between words, music and paint. I hope something here makes its way into your weekend, and that the Musée de Grenoble holds a pleasant surprise.

Enjoy your Saturday, Yamuna, and may the light over the valley be kind.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the fourteenth of November, and this weekend the valley has a good deal on, from candlelit concerts to the first snow on the tops.

Let me begin with something that reads like the seed of a novel. France 3 Alpes tells the story of a woman from Isère, the great-granddaughter of a poilu who was interned in a psychiatric hospital after the First World War. She has chosen to write about him, to give him back his voice. The piece is titled "Ces hommes atteints de maladies de femmes", which tells you something about how the doctors of the day regarded men broken by the trenches. It joins family memory to the forgotten psychological cost of nineteen fourteen to eighteen, and it's the sort of history that novels often teach better than textbooks.

Now to this evening, which is busy, especially in the Grésivaudan. At Froges, in the Église Sainte-Thérèse, there is a concert of Nordic chants from six until seven thirty. A church, voices and, I imagine, a good deal of quiet: it seems made for you. In Pontcharra, from half past five until seven, the Mois du doc presents a screening of the documentary Aurores Boréales. The listing gives no further detail, but it's one for a documentary lover. The two overlap, I'm afraid, so you would have to choose between the voices and the screen.

If you'd rather go later, there's a longer evening on the Plateau des Petites Roches, at La GrAnge, from half past six until eleven. It begins with a Tremplin du Vulnéraire Festival, a showcase for emerging acts, and then a concert by Arash Sarkechik. I can't tell you how far that is from Les Adrets by road, so do check before setting off. And at Le Cheylas, from a quarter past seven until ten, Serge Caillet gives a talk on Monsieur Philippe de Lyon. The listing says little more, but it sounds like a portrait of a Lyon figure, and a talk about a person can be a good way into a period.

Grenoble has a thoughtful thread running through its weekend, around exile. The Migrant'scène festival begins today, Saturday, and Le Dauphiné Libéré describes it as using art and personal encounter to change the way we look at exile. Alongside it, Ici-Grenoble announces an open-air concert by Musique aux frontières, given in support of exiled people. The announcement I have gives no date or venue, so it's worth looking up before you plan anything. Both events share the idea that stories and music can do what statistics can't.

Still in Grenoble, but looking a little further ahead, a few seasonal listings have appeared. The programme for the Grenoble Christmas market has been published by the Journal des Savoie, with animations, concerts and workshops planned for families. Le Dauphiné Libéré has also published a guide to the Festival du cirque in Grenoble, covering the acts, the jury and the staging. The snippet gives no dates, so I can't say when it takes place. And the Dolce Cinema festival is celebrating its twentieth edition, in Grenoble and elsewhere in Isère, according to mesinfos. Again, no dates in what I have, but twenty years is a respectable run for a local festival.

Up in the mountains, Grenoble Mag reports the first snow on Isère's summits, with a call for prudence before the ski resorts open. Only the headline reached me, but it is a pleasing sign that winter is arriving above you in Belledonne. On the practical side of the season, there's a ski swap, a bourse aux skis, today at La Pléiade in Allevard, from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. It's aimed at skiers, but it has the flea-market spirit of rummaging for a bargain, should you fancy a wander.

For a slower outing, Isère Attractivité lists a free exhibition called "Hier, au temps futur", at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse. It opened yesterday and runs until the thirtieth of January, so there's no hurry, and it could make a good winter excursion into the Chartreuse hills. I have no further detail on what's shown, only the title, which is rather lovely in itself.

Closer to home, the Département de l'Isère has a piece on walnut oil from an old mill at Tencin, titled "L'or du vieux moulin". Tencin is close to Les Adrets, and the text I have is thin, but it points to a local producer you might enjoy visiting, particularly with winter cooking in mind.

One event has already passed. Yesterday evening, at five o'clock, the Saint Exupéry media library in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin offered a virtual reality experience called Insider-outsider. The listing is sparse, so I mention it only in case something similar comes round again.

So, a church full of Nordic voices, a documentary, a little music on the plateau, and a long exhibition to look forward to. I hope you find a candle-lit corner of the valley to enjoy this evening.

Good morning, Yamuna. It is Saturday the fourteenth of November, and the last two days have brought a handful of quiet stories and a good crop of things to do close to home, with a lot happening this very evening.

I'll start with a story rather than an event, because it seems made for you. France 3 Alpes has a piece from Isère headlined "Ces hommes atteints de maladies de femmes", which means "men suffering from women's illnesses". It is about a woman who is the great-granddaughter of a poilu, one of the French soldiers of the Great War, who was interned in a psychiatric hospital. She is writing, in her words, to give him back his voice. The title points to the way the psychological damage of the trenches was once labelled and misunderstood, and the story itself sits where family memory meets the forgotten mental toll of nineteen fourteen to eighteen. I only have the outline, but it is the kind of history you often say novels teach better than textbooks, here told through one man in one family. It might even make a good starting point for a conversation with a première class studying war writing, though I'll leave that thought with you.

Now to today, because several things are happening in the Grésivaudan and its surroundings, mostly in the late afternoon and evening, so you could string two together if you felt energetic.

The earliest is in Pontcharra, where a screening of the documentary "Aurores Boréales", the Northern Lights, runs from half past five until seven this evening. It is part of the Mois du doc, the month of documentary film, and the listing gives no further detail about the film or the venue within the town. Given your fondness for documentaries, it may be worth a quick phone call or a look at the town's page before setting off.

A little later, at six o'clock, there is a concert of Nordic chants at the Église Sainte-Thérèse in Froges, running until half past seven. Again the listing is brief, but a church, voices and northern songs make a pleasing evening, and it happens to chime with the northern theme in Pontcharra, though I would not suggest you try to do both, as the timings overlap. Choose by mood: images of light over the Arctic, or voices in a church on a November night.

Also at six thirty, up on the Plateau des Petites Roches, La GrAnge hosts a Tremplin du Vulnéraire Festival, which is a showcase for emerging acts, followed by a concert by Arash Sarkechik. It runs until eleven o'clock. I should be honest that I can't tell you how far this is from Les Adrets by road, and the plateau sits on the far side of the valley, so it is worth checking the journey before committing, particularly as a late finish in November means a drive home in the dark.

Another option this evening, from quarter past seven until ten o'clock, is a talk in Le Cheylas by Serge Caillet on "Monsieur Philippe de Lyon". The listing says nothing more. The name suggests a figure from Lyon, and a talk built around one person might appeal to your taste for history told through people, but I can't say more about who he was or what the talk will cover, so I would treat it as a curiosity to look up rather than a promise.

For something more down to earth, there is a bourse aux skis today in Allevard, at La Pléiade, from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. This is a second-hand ski swap, in the spirit of the flea markets you enjoy, with its own sense of seasonal bustle. It is aimed at skiers, so it will matter only if you or someone in your household needs equipment, but if you fancy a wander through a hall full of people hunting for bargains before winter, it is open all day.

Winter is, in fact, arriving on cue. Grenoble Mag reports that the first snow has fallen on the summits of Isère, and urges caution before the ski resorts open. I only have the headline, so I cannot tell you which peaks or how much, but for those of us living on the slopes of Belledonne it is a reminder that the season is turning. If you walk in the hills, the message is to be careful, as conditions at altitude can change well before the lifts begin turning.

Moving down into Grenoble, there is a cluster of cultural events, several with a thoughtful angle. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Migrant'scène festival begins today, Saturday the fourteenth. It uses art and personal encounter to change how people look at exile. The idea of encounter is what appeals to me: stories told by the people who have lived them, rather than statistics. I don't have the programme, so I can't say whether there are readings, exhibitions or performances, but it seems to be the sort of festival where the arts and storytelling carry the message.

Linked to this, Ici-Grenoble announces an outdoor concert by Musique aux frontières, given in support of exiled people. The snippet gives no date and no venue, so I cannot tell you when or where it will take place, only that it exists and has a humane purpose. If the festival interests you, the organisers' pages may give the details, and the two might well be connected, though I can't confirm that.

For lighter fare, Le Dauphiné Libéré has published a guide to the Festival du cirque in Grenoble, covering the numbers, the jury and the staging. The acts are presumably the heart of it, and the mention of a jury suggests a competition. I don't have the dates, I'm afraid, but if you have never been to a circus festival, it is a rare chance to see live performance of a very different kind from the theatre you usually enjoy, and the staging is clearly part of the appeal.

There is also news of a milestone: the Dolce Cinema festival is celebrating its twentieth edition, in Grenoble and in other places across Isère. The report is short and gives no dates, so I can't say what is showing or when. Twenty years is a good run for a local festival, and since it spreads beyond Grenoble, there may be a screening somewhere near you.

And looking ahead to the Christmas season, the programme for the Grenoble Christmas market of two thousand and twenty-six has been published by jds.fr, with animations, concerts and workshops for families. It is early, but a published programme means you can plan which evenings might suit a concert, or a workshop if you have visitors with children. I don't have the dates or the individual events to hand, so that will need a look at the full listing.

Slightly further out, but with a long life ahead of it, there is an exhibition in the Chartreuse hills. "Hier, au temps futur", which translates roughly as "Yesterday, in the future tense", opened yesterday, the thirteenth of November, at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse, and runs until the thirtieth of January two thousand and twenty-seven. It is free. I know nothing about its content beyond the title, which I rather like, but the long run makes it ideal for a slow winter outing, perhaps combined with a walk if the snow allows, and it means there is no rush to see it this weekend.

Also yesterday, in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, the Saint Exupéry media library offered a virtual reality experience called "Insider-outsider" at five in the afternoon. That has already happened, and the listing gave very little detail, but I mention it because it suggests the media libraries in the valley are worth watching for this sort of event, particularly given the title, which hints at belonging and exclusion, themes close to the exile festival in Grenoble.

Finally, for a producer's story, the Département de l'Isère has a piece called "Huile de noix de Tencin : l'or du vieux moulin", about walnut oil from an old mill in Tencin, which is very close to Les Adrets. The text I have is thin, so I can't tell you whether the mill sells directly or at which markets, but the headline calls the oil gold from the old mill, and in walnut country that is not an exaggeration. If you enjoy local producers, it may be worth finding out whether you can visit or buy from the mill itself, especially as winter cooking and gifts are not far off.

So that is the picture: a Great War story with a family at its heart, a busy Saturday evening in the valley, a festival in Grenoble giving voice to exile, and snow on the tops reminding us what season we are in. I hope you find something that suits your day, Yamuna, and that it is a gentle one.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with a Welsh pilgrimage site, a little Atwood and a cheering full house in Turkey for good measure.

Let me begin with the one that dominates the news, a Hamlet you could discuss with première. Thom Yorke's Hamlet Hail to the Thief has opened at the Barbican in London, a mash-up of Shakespeare's play with Radiohead's music, and the reviews arrived all at once. The Times calls it a taut collision between the Bard and Radiohead. London Theatre describes it as an atmospheric rush, and the critic's emphasis is on how fast-moving it is. Alexis Petridis, writing in The Guardian, is more mixed in tone. His headline suggests it could have been rotten but redeems what he calls Radiohead's record that got away. Time Out's headline takes on the sceptics directly, insisting it is not Hamlet dumbed down for 6Music dads. Only that headline came through, so I can't tell you how the argument unfolds. The Stage and southlondon.co.uk have also reviewed it, though I don't have their verdicts.

For a teacher, the useful point is that this is a reworking and not the text itself. That makes it good material for a reception exercise. You could ask students what a production keeps, what it sacrifices, and what music can do that Shakespeare's verse cannot, or perhaps does differently. Setting a critic's praise for pace beside another's reservations is a lovely way to teach them that reviews are arguments, with evidence and a point of view, which is rather the skill you want them to bring to their own essays.

Two other Hamlets turned up as well, both smaller. Front Mezz Junkies reviews Raoul Bhaneja's one-man production, Hamlet solo, and praises the actor's talent in its headline. Only a brief text came through, but a single performer carrying every role is an intriguing prompt for discussing interpretation. Who does the actor become when the court, the ghost and Ophelia are all one body and one voice? Meanwhile BroadwayWorld reports that COPE Productions will present See What I See, a Sapphic reimagining of Hamlet, at Madame X. No dates were given, so it is one to watch for rather than to plan around. Taken together with the Barbican, these give you three very different modern answers to the question of what the play is for.

Staying with the 2027 session, there is some good news for Under Milk Wood, which I think you will enjoy. The Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. Swansea Bay News adds the practical detail: the Boathouse is closed until the new year while seventy-seven thousand pounds is spent on it. I'd rather not guess at how those two reports fit together, but the picture is clear enough. The place where Thomas wrote is being looked after, and it will reopen. That is a lovely, evocative link for class. Under Milk Wood is a play for voices, written to be heard, and it is rooted in a very particular small town on the water. Showing students the setting, and perhaps asking how much of Llareggub they can find in a real estuary village, is an easy and rewarding way in. If anyone is planning a trip to Wales, the new year looks like the moment.

There is more good news on the stage side. Foro3D reports that Kocaeli Theatres premiered Twelfth Night in its Grand Hall to a full house, and the report is dated the thirteenth of November. The piece is brief, but it is pleasing to know that a set play is drawing a packed audience in Turkey. It is a nice thing to mention to seconde or première, a reminder that Shakespeare's comedy of disguise and longing is being performed far beyond the places they might imagine.

Now for the oral themes, where Margaret Atwood has quietly been in the headlines. AOL carries a piece asking whether we are on the road to Gilead, the world of The Handmaid's Tale, and the headline says Atwood does not say no. Only the headline is available, so I can't tell you what she actually said, but as a prompt it is interesting. Students working on dystopias often ask whether the novel is a warning or a prediction, and Atwood's own reluctance to rule things out is a conversation starter in its own right. A brief item from the Miami Herald reports that Jess Gibson spoke about her first book in conversation with her mother, Margaret Atwood, at the Miami Book Fair. The text is short, but it gives an author-centred angle, a glimpse of Atwood as a parent and writer sharing a stage. Finally, Britannica has an explainer asking how Atwood reinterpreted the historical settler Susanna Moodie in The Journals of Susanna Moodie. Again I only have the question, not the answer, but it points to something useful: Atwood habitually takes a real historical figure and rewrites her through fiction. That is the kind of link between history and imagination you enjoy, and it might help students see that The Handmaid's Tale, too, is built from historical fact.

One last item sits outside the programme, but it is a book for the pile. The Guardian reviews One for Sorrow by Favel Parrett, and the headline calls it an affecting novel that builds to a devastating climax. I only have the headline, so that's the whole of what I can say, but it may be one for your own reading.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope the weekend brings you a good book and a little time to enjoy it.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the news, with a few welcome stops in Wales, Canada and Miami along the way, and most of it is useful for the BFI classroom.

Let me start with the big one, because five or six outlets have covered it at once. Thom Yorke's Hamlet Hail to the Thief is running at the Barbican Theatre in London, and it is a Shakespeare and Radiohead mash-up. Hamlet is on the session twenty twenty-seven programme, so a production like this is a live example of how the play gets reworked and reimagined, which is exactly the sort of reception material that gives seconde and première something to argue about.

The reviews are worth reading side by side, because the headlines alone already disagree in an interesting way. The Times calls it a taut collision between the Bard and Radiohead. That word "taut" suggests something tightly strung, with the two sources pulling against each other. London Theatre is more breathless, describing it as an atmospheric rush, and the critic there finds it fast-moving. Alexis Petridis, writing in The Guardian, is a little more guarded. His review says the show could have been rotten, and finds it rotten in places, but ultimately redeeming. He also frames it around what he calls Radiohead's record that got away, so he is writing as much about the music as the theatre. Then Time Out has perhaps the most quotable headline of the lot: "It's not Hamlet dumbed down for 6Music dads." That one is interesting for a teacher, because it shows the reviewer anticipating a suspicion, that putting Hamlet next to a rock band must mean simplifying it, and pushing back against it. The Stage and southlondon.co.uk have also reviewed it. I only have the fact of those reviews, not their verdicts, so I would read them before quoting them to anyone.

A word of caution that applies to all of these. This is a reworking, not the text itself. The critics are responding to a piece of theatre built on Hamlet, and none of them is telling you what Shakespeare wrote. For the classroom, I think that is the strength of it. You could give a première group the headlines alone, with no review text, and ask them to predict what each critic found good or bad. Then you could read the reviews and see whether they guessed right. A second exercise would be to ask what a production gains and loses by pairing Shakespeare with modern music, which leads naturally into the question of what in Hamlet is already musical: the rhythm of the soliloquies, the songs of Ophelia, the sense of a mind going round and round the same thought. If any pupils are Radiohead listeners, or have parents who are, this could be a very easy way into the play. And since you enjoy the links between the arts, it is a pleasing example of one form talking to another.

Two other Hamlet stagings turned up in the same stretch, both smaller in scale. The first is Hamlet solo, a one-man production by Raoul Bhaneja. The review, from front mezz junkies, praises the actor's extraordinary talent in its headline, and I only have that headline and a very short text. Even so, the idea is rich for teaching. A single actor has to play every voice in the play, so the production is a question in itself: how do you tell Claudius from Gertrude, or Polonius from Laertes, with one body and one voice? It could be a good prompt for pupils to try something similar with a short scene, perhaps the closet scene, and notice how much a change of posture or pace does the work of a change of character.

The second is a announcement from BroadwayWorld. COPE Productions will present See What I See, described as a sapphic reimagining of Hamlet, at Madame X. The piece gives no dates, so it is more a signpost than something you could plan around. But it adds to the picture of Hamlet being a play that each generation pulls into its own shape. Taken together with the Barbican production and the solo version, you have three very different answers to the question of what Hamlet is for, which is a good conversation for an oral or an essay on interpretation.

Moving from Denmark to Turkey would be a leap I cannot quite support with the facts I have, so let me simply say that there is cheerful news about another set play. Foro3D reports that Kocaeli Theatres premiered Twelfth Night in its Grand Hall to a full house, with the report dated the thirteenth of November. The article is brief, but I like it for what it is: a set text reaching a live audience, and a full house at that. For pupils who think of Shakespeare as something that lives in a school anthology, it is nice evidence that a comedy about disguise, longing and mistaken identity still fills a hall. It is also a good moment to remind them that Twelfth Night was written to be watched, which might change how they read Viola's speeches.

Now to Wales, and here the news is warm and concrete. The Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. Swansea Bay News gives more detail on the practical side. The Boathouse is closed until the new year while seventy-seven thousand pounds is spent on it. I cannot tell you from what I have exactly what the work involves, so I will not guess at it. But the headline asks what the money is buying, and that would be worth checking if you want to tell your class. The two reports sit comfortably together: one speaks of the larger investment, the other puts a figure on the current closure and the work it pays for.

Under Milk Wood is on the session twenty twenty-seven programme, and the Boathouse is a place where Thomas wrote, so there is a lovely link here between a real, physical room and one of the most musical pieces of prose drama in the language. That is the kind of passage you like, I think: language that is meant to be heard, with the sea and the town and the sleeping voices all in it. For a class, the closure is almost a useful prompt in itself. Pupils cannot visit just now, so you might ask them to imagine the place from the text alone, then later compare it with photographs or a virtual visit once the building reopens. Another idea would be to read the opening of Under Milk Wood aloud, in the dark if you can manage it, and ask them to draw what they hear before they see any images. It also fits your own taste for local culture, even if this particular local culture is a long way from the Grésivaudan.

The third group of stories concerns Margaret Atwood, and here I have to be honest about how little text came through. For The Handmaid's Tale, which is one of the oral themes, there are three pieces. The first is an AOL article asking whether we are on the road to Gilead, with Atwood's response. Its headline says she does not say no. That is all I have, but it is a ready-made discussion question for an oral class: why do dystopias keep being compared with the present, and what does Atwood herself seem to accept or refuse in that comparison? You could pair it with the novel's own claim that nothing in it is invented from nothing, though I would check that against her own words before quoting it.

The second is from the Miami Herald. Jess Gibson talked about her first book in conversation with her mother, Margaret Atwood, at the Miami Book Fair. The text is short, so the detail is limited, but it gives you an author-focused angle, with Atwood seen as a mother and a fellow writer rather than as the voice behind Gilead. That could suit a gentler lesson, perhaps on how writers talk about their work in public, which is a useful skill for pupils preparing an oral.

The third is a Britannica explainer asking how Atwood reinterpreted Susanna Moodie in The Journals of Susanna Moodie. Moodie was a historical settler, and Atwood's book reimagines her. Again, only the question came through. But it is the sort of link you enjoy, where fiction and history meet and a real life is retold as poetry and story. It could show pupils that Atwood's habit of rewriting existing material did not begin with The Handmaid's Tale, and it sets up a good question about how novelists can teach history differently from textbooks.

One last item is outside the programme. The Guardian reviews One for Sorrow, a novel by Favel Parrett, and its headline calls it affecting and says it builds to a devastating climax. I have nothing beyond that, and it is not on any BFI list, so I mention it only as a possible personal read for you, given your fondness for strong narrators and novels that move you.

If I had to pick two things to do with all this, they would be these. First, take the Hamlet Hail to the Thief reviews into class as a small lesson on how critics argue, using the headlines as a starting point. Second, keep an eye on the Boathouse for when it reopens after the new year. Everything else is a pleasant extra, and a reminder that these texts are still being staged, argued over and loved.

That is the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope your Friday has a little poetry in it.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter, more reflective stretch in France today, with a good deal from the world of schools, a little wonder from space, and a handful of phrases you might enjoy.

I'll start with remembrance. On Friday, the thirteenth of November, ceremonies were held at the sites of the 2015 Paris attacks, eleven years on, as franceinfo explains. In the evening, the association Life for Paris invited the public to a citizen tribute at the 13-Novembre memorial garden, to remember all victims of terrorism, not only those of that night.

Now to schools, which have been busy. Teachers and heads have had a rough few days. Franceinfo reports that Paris lycée heads are describing real despair as blockades disrupt their schools. Two of those interviewed call the situation untenable, and one asks how on earth anyone is meant to catch up afterwards. The head teachers' union, SNPDEN-Unsa, called on principals to gather outside their schools on Friday at three in the afternoon. Alongside this, the teaching unions have reacted angrily to remarks by the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, who spoke of the "complicity" of some education staff in the violence seen during the recent lycée protests. It's a heated exchange, but I mention it because it touches daily school life directly. The Ministry of National Education also announced three hoax bomb alerts, at schools in the Bouches-du-Rhône, the Aisne and the Jura. They affected the Lycée Don Bosco in Marseille, the IUT in Laon and schools in Morez.

On a more practical note, a worldwide Microsoft outage since Thursday evening has disrupted Outlook and other services for millions of people. Franceinfo spoke to teachers, carers and trainers, one of whom called it "chômage technique", a sort of enforced technical downtime. If your school inbox has been strangely silent, you may well know why.

For something more human, franceinfo has a portrait by the journalist Tristan Waleckx, who spent forty-eight hours in the northern neighbourhoods of Marseille. The headline quotes a resident: young people there, it says, have no right to make mistakes. It's a portrait of daily life rather than an argument, and it sounds like the kind of piece that gives you a narrator's-eye view of a place.

Now for the good news. The European Space Agency has published its first large release of images and data from the Euclid telescope, launched in 2023. It shows hundreds of millions of galaxies, which is a rather staggering sentence to say aloud. And HugoDécrypte has a video about a seventeen-year-old Australian who was found alive after six days lost in the bush. The details are thin, but it's a rare and cheering survival story.

On the cultural side, franceinfo reports on a small, intimate exhibition at the MAD, the decorative arts museum in Paris, honouring Yohan Serfaty, the designer behind the label Y.Project. He trained in political science before turning to fashion, and the show focuses on his craft-led work in leather and bespoke tailoring. It's described as a tribute to a singular, rather forgotten creator. No dates were given, so do check before you plan anything. The Local France also has a preview of French films with English subtitles for December. It includes a special screening of La Haine, with the director present, marking the eleventh anniversary of the film club L'Âge d'Or. There are also two films by Leos Carax and some Christmas classics. The piece doesn't say where the screening is, so that's one to look up. And for a light-hearted finish to the television week, La Mire's daily zapping for the twelfth of November covers the Armistice commemoration, an anniversary segment, and a history teacher in the Aisne. It's quick and easy, though some segments do touch on politics.

Now, three bits of French for your pupils, all from The Local France. The first is "Tu parles !", which is not a literal "you're talking". It's a retort that signals scepticism or irony, rather like "Yeah, right!" in English. The second is "être à la bourre", meaning to be running late, a nice informal alternative to the textbook phrase. And the third is "lacrymo", the slang for tear gas, short for lacrymogène. It has been much discussed in France lately, so it may be turning up in conversation.

Finally, a practical note if you're planning travel. The Local France reports that several British travellers have been wrongly accused of overstaying the EU's ninety-day allowance during the chaotic start of the new EES biometric border checks. If you or any of your British-section colleagues are crossing borders soon, it's worth keeping a record of your entry dates and allowing extra time.

That's all for today, Yamuna, and I hope your Saturday brings a good book, a warm drink and not a single email.
france.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is your gentle round-up of France for this Saturday, the fourteenth of November, with a little remembrance, a little wonder, a good deal about schools, and some words and films to take away with you.

Let me begin with two pieces that are about people rather than politics. The first comes from franceinfo, where the journalist Tristan Waleckx spent forty-eight hours in the northern neighbourhoods of Marseille and shares the daily lives of the residents he met. The headline is a quotation, and it says, roughly, that young people from working-class neighbourhoods do not have the right to make mistakes. It is a human portrait rather than an argument, and that is why I mention it. If you like fiction that lets you step into a place without needing to know it first, this kind of reporting works in a similar way, through voices and small details of a day.

The second is about remembrance. Yesterday, Friday the thirteenth of November, commemorative ceremonies took place at the sites of the Paris attacks of 2015. In the evening, the association Life for Paris invited the public to a citizen tribute at the thirteenth of November memorial garden, to remember all victims of terrorism. franceinfo set out how the day was to unfold. It is a quiet anniversary, and a reminder of how much of the country's memory is now held in places like that garden, where anyone can simply come and stand for a while.

Now for something brighter, and I think you will like these. The European Space Agency has published its first large release of images and data from the Euclid telescope, which was launched in two thousand and twenty-three. The pictures show hundreds of millions of galaxies. It is hard to hold a number like that in the mind, and perhaps that is the point. It is science, but it is also close to poetry, a vast night sky laid out in detail, and it belongs to everyone rather than to any one country. I can imagine a few lines of Hardy or Woolf sitting very comfortably beside it.

Then a survival story with a happy ending. HugoDécrypte, in its daily video round-up, reports that a seventeen-year-old Australian has been found alive after six days lost in the bush. The details in the text are thin, so I will not embroider them, but it is a rare and uplifting piece of news, and one that would not look out of place at the start of an adventure novel, only here it ended well.

Let me turn to school life, because several stories this weekend touch on it directly, and you will recognise some of it.

First, the small and slightly worrying. The Ministry of National Education has announced three hoax bomb alerts at schools, in the Bouches-du-Rhône, the Aisne and the Jura. The affected sites include the Lycée Don Bosco in Marseille, the IUT in Laon, and schools in Morez. The ministry describes them as false alerts, which means nobody was in danger, but I know such things still disrupt a day and unsettle staff and pupils.

Second, a more widespread disruption of a very modern kind. A worldwide Microsoft outage, which began on Thursday evening, has affected Outlook and other services for millions of people. franceinfo spoke to teachers, carers and trainers about how it is changing their working days, and one of them put it in a phrase that made me smile ruefully: "C'est chômage technique", which you might render as "we're effectively laid off by the technology". If you have found your school email behaving oddly, you were evidently in good company. It is a small reminder of how much of a teacher's day, the sending of texts, the sharing of documents, the arranging of meetings, now travels through a few screens.

Third, and more serious, are the protests and blockades at lycées. I will keep this to the school side of it. franceinfo has interviews with Paris headteachers describing their despair as blockades disrupt their schools. One asks, "Comment voulez-vous qu'on rattrape ça ?", in other words, how do you expect us to catch up on all this? Two of the heads interviewed call the situation untenable. The head teachers' union, SNPDEN-Unsa, called on principals to gather outside their own schools on Friday at three in the afternoon. What I find telling here is the point of view. We so often hear about these events from the pupils or the politicians, and here it is the people responsible for the building, the timetable and the exams, who are trying to keep everything together and wondering how the lost time can be made up.

Alongside that, there is a row involving teachers' unions. Teaching unions have reacted angrily after the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said that some Éducation nationale staff were complicit in the violence during the recent lycée protests. The unions are furious at the word "complicity". It is a political dispute, so I will not take it any further than that, but I mention it because it bears on how teachers feel they are seen, and because it may well come up in the staff room.

Now, since you work in languages, let me offer a little vocabulary, because The Local France has given us three useful items this week.

The first is the expression of the day, "Tu parles !". It is a retort that signals scepticism or irony, rather than simply stating the obvious. So when someone says "tu parles !", they are not literally telling you that you are speaking. They mean something closer to "yeah, right" or "you must be joking". It is the sort of idiom that pupils like, because it shows how much French is carried in tone, and how a phrase can say the opposite of what its words suggest. Your classes might enjoy hunting for English equivalents that do the same thing.

The second is another expression of the day, "être à la bourre", which means to be running late. It is informal, lively, and very much a phrase of daily life. You could imagine it sliding into a lesson on idioms about time, set beside "to be behind the clock" or "to be running behind", and asking pupils which sounds more vivid.

The third is the word of the day, "lacrymo", the slang for tear gas, a word which has been much discussed in France recently. It is a shortened form of "lacrymogène", the adjective that goes with "gaz", and it is a good example of how French likes to clip long words into friendly, short ones. The text is thin, so I will leave it there, but it makes a good example of how slang follows the news.

On to culture, where there are two pieces that I think will suit you, and one that is light television.

At the MAD, the museum of decorative arts in Paris, there is an intimate exhibition called "Hommage à Yohan Serfaty". It honours a fashion designer who created the label Y.Project, and who trained in political science before turning to fashion. franceinfo describes him as a singular and somewhat forgotten creator, and the exhibition focuses on his craft-led work, in leather and in bespoke tailoring. I like the idea of it, an overlooked maker being given a quiet, careful tribute, and the emphasis on hands and materials rather than on glamour. The piece gives no dates, so you would want to check the museum's own information before planning a visit.

For film lovers, The Local France has a preview of French films with English subtitles to watch in December. It includes a special screening of "La Haine", marking the eleventh anniversary of the film club L'Âge d'Or, with the director present. There are also two films by Leos Carax, and some Christmas classics. The piece does not say where the screenings are, so again that is something to look up. I know cinema news is not your main interest, but a film club with a director in the room for a discussion is the kind of evening that might suit you, and "La Haine" is a film that many teachers use to talk about language, place and young people's voices.

And the light television item. La Mire has published its daily zapping of French television for the twelfth of November. It covers the Armistice commemoration, an anniversary segment connected with Verdun, and a history teacher in the Aisne. It is quick and playful, though some segments touch on politics, so you can skip those. A history teacher in front of the cameras is perhaps a nice companion to everything else this morning about schools.

Finally, something practical for anyone in your position, as a British teacher living in France who may be planning trips. The Local France reports that several British travellers say they were wrongly accused of overstaying the European Union's ninety-day allowance, after getting caught up in the chaotic start of the new EES biometric border checks. They describe confusion at the border, and being treated as though they had stayed too long when they had not. The article does not say more than that, but if you or friends and family are travelling on a British passport, it is worth keeping your dates and travel records somewhere easy to find, and allowing extra time at the border.

So that is the news from France this morning: stars and survivors, schools under strain, and a handful of good words to carry into your next lesson, and I hope the day treats you kindly, whether you spend it at a market in the valley or simply with a good book by the window.
