Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a bookish, painterly streak, with a few small kindnesses tucked in alongside.

Let me start with the writer everyone is talking about. M John Harrison, at eighty-one, is the oldest person ever to win the Booker Prize, and he has been wonderfully candid in interviews. The Bookseller caught him on age and on his long refusal of genre labels, with the line "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." The i Paper has him in more mischievous mood: "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." And The Irish Times offers the warmest version, in which he describes lying awake most of the night thinking, "This is extraordinary." It's rare to hear a prizewinner sound so delighted and so unbothered at once. The Guardian, in an editorial, calls the win a new frontier for science fiction, and places the book within the wider history of the genre. If you want something to show your première students, it's a good example of a writer who simply wouldn't be filed under one heading, and was recognised anyway.

Staying with the idea of things finally being seen, there's a lovely run of stories from the art world. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that, during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found a technique not seen before, and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The piece is only a short teaser so far, but the idea of Michelangelo slipping himself into that vast scene is hard to resist.

Beaux Arts also tells us that Metz is hosting the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was a self-taught painter who worked as a cleaner, and the exhibition aims to show the great painter behind the legend, on her own terms. It reads almost like a novel waiting to be written, though perhaps one already has been.

And from Good News Network, a story that belongs in a novel too. A woman named Betsy was clearing out an East Village apartment with her elderly aunt, when the aunt remarked that there was a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet. Those few words led to the painting's joyful rediscovery. I rather like that the whole thing began with a sentence, almost thrown away.

That theme of rediscovery runs through a few history stories as well. Good News Network reports that a handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Junior's "I Have a Dream" speech, written on the morning of the march to the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after six decades. It was found in a desk drawer, and it is heavily revised, which shows just how carefully he worked on his words. It's a rare chance to watch a famous text in the making, and it would make a fine companion to a close reading of the speech itself.

Also from Good News Network, a one hundred and three-year-old D-Day veteran has been reunited with his war medals, in time for Remembrance Day. An amateur historian of the Second World War traced him through his military record and brought them back. It's a quiet, moving piece about memory being honoured while there is still someone to hold it.

Another story from the same outlet concerns Rodney Anderson, an Englishman of eighty-one, who has found his long-lost Canadian relatives. A wartime encounter had separated the two families for more than eighty years, and a family-tree search finally brought them together. Eight decades is a long time to wait for a missing chapter.

And from Upworthy, a neat link between past and present. In eighteen eighty-five, Gertrude Bustill Mossell launched a newspaper column devoted to the achievements and struggles of Black women. The piece connects her to the writing career of Peggy Scott, the character in The Gilded Age. It's brief, but it points to a real woman who made her own rules, which could be a useful way into the history behind the drama.

Closer to the classroom, the Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. The details aren't in the report I have, but it's good news for the place where so much of that voice took shape, and with Under Milk Wood on your twenty twenty-seven session, a timely one.

Now a few gentler stories, about people looking after one another. Positivr tells of a florist in Cuincy, near Lille, who, rather than throwing away her unsold All Saints' chrysanthemums, places them on forgotten graves in the cemetery. Nobody had asked her to, and it is such a small and generous act, thinking of those whom no one visits.

In Bradley, Illinois, Gretchen Sollo turned one hundred, and Good News Network says she was given her first ever surprise birthday party. It was thrown by the staff at the Lowe's store, where she walks every day and has become something of a mother figure. A hundred years, and the party came from the people she greets on her daily rounds.

Last, and rather practical. Upworthy reports that Josh Staub, the animator who worked on Frozen, has launched an interactive app for learning American Sign Language. He built it as a labour of love, working with Deaf animators, engineers and other collaborators, and he has promised to keep it free forever. It's a concrete gift to learners, and a good model of making something with the community it serves rather than merely for it.

That's the good news for today, and I hope some of it follows you up the hill to Les Adrets.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a gentle couple of days for good news, and a surprising amount of it is about words, paintings and people who were finally given their due.

Let me begin with the story that several outlets are circling, because it is a lovely one for a literature teacher. M John Harrison has won the Booker Prize at the age of eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner in the prize's history. What I enjoy most is the number of different interviews, because each one catches a slightly different note of the same man.

The Bookseller talked to him about age, writing and his long refusal of genre labels. His line there is wonderfully disarming: "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." There is something very human in that, the sense that a person can be eighty-one on the calendar and still carry the same restless young mind inside. It would make a fine opening for a conversation with your students about how writers see themselves, and how little the inner voice seems to age.

The i Paper caught him in a more mischievous mood. Its headline has him saying, "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." It is said with a kind of cheerful bluntness, and it turns late recognition into a licence for freedom rather than a final bow. Then The Irish Times gives us the warmer, more tender version. He describes lying awake for much of the night, thinking, "This is extraordinary." I rather love that. After a lifetime of writing, the astonishment is still fresh, and he is still allowed to be amazed by it.

Finally, The Guardian has an editorial on the win, framing it as a new frontier for science fiction. It places the winning novel within the wider history and development of the genre, and it reads the prize as a sign that the old walls between the literary and the speculative may be thinning. Given that Harrison himself has spent a career resisting the labels, there is a pleasing irony in a prize that seems to have made the labels matter a little less. If you wanted a small classroom exercise, you could set the four voices side by side, the playful, the defiant, the wondering and the analytical, and ask which tells you the most about the writer.

From one kind of late recognition to another, and now to painting. There is a run of art stories this morning that feel almost like chapters in a novel.

The one I would start with comes from Good News Network. A woman named Betsy was clearing out an East Village apartment with her elderly aunt, when the aunt said, almost in passing, that there was a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet. It is the sort of sentence that might open a story. The piece traces how that offhand remark led to the painting's joyful rediscovery. I like that it began with spoken words, a throwaway line in a cluttered flat, and ended with a painting coming back into the light. It has the shape of a short story, with the unremarkable setting, the quiet revelation and the sense that the world is still full of things waiting behind closet doors.

Beaux Arts Magazine has two stories that will interest you. The first concerns the Sistine Chapel. During the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment, conservators have reportedly found a technique not seen before, and a hidden self-portrait by the artist. I should say that the piece I have is only a short teaser, so the details are thin, and I would treat it as a promising lead rather than a full account. But even as a hint, it is striking. A painting that has been looked at by millions for nearly five centuries is still, it seems, giving up secrets to those who clean it patiently. For anyone who loves the making of a work as much as the work itself, that is a quiet thrill.

The second is closer to your own tastes, I suspect. In Metz, the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis has opened. She lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two, and she was a self-taught painter who earned her living as a cleaner. Beaux Arts Magazine says the exhibition reveals the great painter behind the legend. That phrase matters, because for a long time her story has been told as a legend, the humble cleaner who painted, rather than as the work of an artist taken seriously on her own terms. A full retrospective is a way of correcting that. It is a good example of an overlooked woman finally being seen, and it would sit very naturally beside the novels and narrators you love, where the person nobody noticed turns out to hold the whole story. Metz is not far in the grand scheme of things, so it may be worth keeping in mind for a future outing.

Let me turn now to history, and to the way a single page, or a single medal, can carry a whole era.

Good News Network reports that a handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Junior's "I Have a Dream" speech has resurfaced after six decades, coming out of a desk drawer. It was written on the morning of the march at the Lincoln Memorial, and what makes it so remarkable is the heavy revision. You can see the crossings-out, the changes, the care. We tend to think of that speech as a flood of inspired oratory, and here is evidence of a writer at work, weighing and reshaping each phrase on the very day. For a teacher of English, that is gold. It is rare to see a famous text in the act of being made, and it makes a quiet argument for drafting, for patience, and for the idea that the words that move us are usually the product of labour as well as inspiration.

On a more personal scale, the same outlet tells the story of a one hundred and three year old D-Day veteran who has been reunited with his war medals. They were returned in time for Remembrance Day, after an amateur historian of the Second World War traced him through his military record. There is something very moving about the patience of that kind of research, someone sitting with records and names until a lost object finds its owner again. At one hundred and three, he is among the very last who can hold such things in his own hands. It is history as it really lives, in one man's story rather than in a chapter of a textbook.

Upworthy adds a link between past and present that feels made for the classroom. In eighteen eighty-five, Gertrude Bustill Mossell launched a column dedicated to the achievements and struggles of Black women. The piece draws a line from her to the writing career of Peggy Scott, the character in The Gilded Age. The text I have is brief, so I will not claim more than that, but the connection is neat. A fictional journalist on screen echoes a real woman who made her own rules on the page, and it is a nice example of fiction opening a door onto real history, which I know is something you value.

Staying with writers, there is a little cultural good news from south-west Wales. The Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. With Under Milk Wood on the list for the 2027 session, the timing feels especially kind. That play for voices, with its musical, sensuous language, is a perfect text for reading aloud, and it is good to know that the place where its author lived and worked is being looked after. I do not have the figures or the plans, only the news that the funding is in place, but that is already worth celebrating.

Now for the gentler, smaller stories, the ones that remind us how much goodness happens quietly, in ordinary places.

In France, in Cuincy, near Lille, Positivr tells of a florist who would normally have thrown away her unsold flowers after All Saints'. Instead, she places them on the forgotten graves in the cemetery, the ones nobody has visited. It is a small and very concrete act of care. Those flowers would have been waste, and instead they say, to people who have long since been left alone, that someone still notices. I find it touching in a way that reminds me of a good short story, one image doing all the work. The cemetery on the morning after must have looked quite different.

Across the Atlantic, in Bradley, Illinois, Good News Network introduces us to Gretchen Sollo, who has just turned one hundred. She walks daily through her local Lowe's, and the staff there have come to know her so well that they threw her a surprise birthday party. It was her first ever birthday party. Think about that for a moment. A hundred years, and it took the people she greets on her daily walk to give her the celebration. It is a lovely portrait of the unexpected communities that form around routine, and she has been fondly dubbed the store mom. As a character she would not be out of place in a warm novel.

Another human story from Good News Network concerns Rodney Anderson, an eighty-one year old Englishman. A wartime encounter, a tryst, as the piece calls it, divided his family for more than eighty years. With the help of a family-tree search, he has now found his long-lost Canadian relatives, and two families are united. Anyone who loves novels about secrets and inheritance will recognise the architecture of this story, the hidden event in the past, the slow search and the reunion. Here, happily, it ends in warmth rather than tragedy. And it is a reminder that the Second World War is still unfolding in people's lives, decades on.

My last story is about access and education, and it is concrete in the best way. Upworthy reports that Josh Staub, the animator who worked on Frozen, has launched an interactive app for learning American Sign Language. He made it as a labour of love, working with Deaf animators, engineers and other collaborators, and he has promised to keep it free forever. I like that it was made with the community it serves, and that the promise is about keeping it free for good, rather than only for a launch period. For a teacher, a tool like this is a quiet gift. Learning another language, in this case a visual one, is something you understand deeply, and it is good to see one made freely available to anyone who wants to try.

Taken together, there is a common thread in all of this. A line in a closet, a draft in a drawer, a medal traced through a record, a flower on a forgotten grave. Each story is about something that was overlooked and then, through patience or kindness, noticed at last.

That is all for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you as gently as these stories treat their characters.

Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Saturday, the fourteenth of November.

Let's begin with paintings and the stories behind them. Hyperallergic has a piece on James Cahill's new book, which takes David Hockney's portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman as its starting point. It tells the story of two friends who helped shape the cultural life of Los Angeles in the nineteen-sixties, so it's a painting and a richly told human story together. Also from Hyperallergic, El Museo del Barrio is restaging Papo Colo's "Octopus and Others", a show first seen four decades ago that pairs text and image. It's a rare chance to see how a poet and an artist worked together, on the page and on the wall.

From Rome, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found an unprecedented technique, and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The report is only a short teaser so far, but it's tantalising. The same magazine also tells the legend of Nicolas Flamel, in an exhibition called "Nicolas Flamel, alchimiste de papier". It follows the alchemist from the philosopher's stone all the way to its echoes in the Harry Potter saga, which is a fine example of a historical figure drifting into fiction.

Now to the world of books. M John Harrison, who has won the Booker Prize at eighty-one, has been talking to two papers, and the two interviews make a nice pair. In The i Paper, he says, rather magnificently, that he is going to die soon and can now do what he likes. In The Irish Times, the tone is warmer and more private: he describes lying awake most of the night thinking, "This is extraordinary." Late recognition, then, taken with candour and a little wonder.

For lovers of a good sentence, The Paris Review's November Bookmarks has arrived. It's a selection of passages underlined in new releases, under the title "A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room". It's a lovely title, and a good reading list for slow Saturday mornings.

Some good news next. Good News Network reports that a handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Junior's "I Have a Dream" speech, written on the morning of the march to the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after sixty years, from a desk drawer. The pages are heavily revised, which shows how carefully he worked on his words. It's a rare chance to watch a famous text in the making, and one your pupils might enjoy. In the same spirit, there's a gentler story of family history. Rodney Anderson, an eighty-one-year-old Englishman, has found his long-lost Canadian relatives with the help of a family-tree search, after a wartime encounter divided the families for eight decades. And from the video news, HugoDécrypte tells of a seventeen-year-old Australian found alive after six days lost in the bush. The details are thin, but the ending is a happy one.

Turning to music, The Guardian has two reviews. The first is of a new period-instrument recording of Handel's Giulio Cesare in Egitto by Il Pomo d'Oro, with Orliński and Sabine Devieilhe. The reviewer is full of praise for Devieilhe's Cleopatra, saying she could make stones weep, and also for the dramatic energy of the whole performance. The second comes from the Royal Festival Hall in London, where the Philharmonia played Strauss and Mozart, with Emanuel Ax as soloist. On the podium was Manfred Honeck, the orchestra's incoming principal conductor, who gave what the reviewer calls a scorching taste of things to come. It's a warm, well-written review, and it sets out Mahler's idea of tradition.

Now a little corner for your terminale and the BFI. The Barbican has been staging Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a production drawing on Shakespeare's Hamlet, and southlondon.co.uk has a review. Since Hamlet is on the twenty twenty-seven programme, it may offer some ideas for teaching and staging. And AOL carries a piece asking whether we are on the road to Gilead, the dystopia of The Handmaid's Tale, with Margaret Atwood's response. Only the headline came through, but it points straight at one of your oral themes, and you may want to read the whole thing.

Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré says the Migrant'scène festival opens in Grenoble today, Saturday the fourteenth of November. It uses art and personal encounter to change how people see exile, which sounds thoughtful and well worth a look. And looking ahead to the season, jds.fr has published the programme for the Grenoble Christmas market of twenty twenty-six, with animations, concerts and workshops for families. It's a useful one to keep for a December outing.

Last, for the cinema-minded. The Local France has a preview of French films with English subtitles to see in December. It includes a special screening of La Haine, with the director present, to mark the eleventh anniversary of the film club L'Âge d'Or, along with two Leos Carax films and some Christmas classics. The piece doesn't say where the screenings are, but it's one to check.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope your Saturday has good light over Belledonne, a book within reach, and at least one perfect sentence.
